Ratios between the accuracy of tests when some profiles are never verified

Source: R/bounds.R
accuracy_ratios.Rd

Gives, for each pair of tests (or rules), the ratio of their sensitivities and the ratio of their false positive rates (one minus the specificity). Unlike the absolute accuracy, these ratios are estimated by the data even when some response profiles are never verified (Alonzo, 2005; Pepe and Alonzo, 2001; Schatzkin et al., 1987).

Usage

accuracy_ratios(fit, rules = fit@data@tests, odds_ratio = NULL, level = 0.95)

Arguments

fit

A model fitted with baysesp() and saturated().

rules

Rules or test names, see rule_accuracy(). By default, the individual tests.

odds_ratio

The odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same response profile, \(\exp(\beta)\): a single positive number (one value only; to compare several values, call the function once for each). 1 means that verification does not depend on the disease status (missing at random); values above 1 mean that the diseased are verified more often. The default, NULL, uses 1 for a model fitted with verification = mar(), and gives an error for a model fitted with verification = mnar(), for which a value must be given.

level

Probability of the credible intervals.

Value

A data frame with one row per ratio and pair of rules and columns quantity, mean, median, lower, upper and probability, the posterior probability that the ratio is greater than 1: for rTPR, that the first rule is more sensitive; for rFPR, that it is less specific. Only the rules that declare no never-verified profile positive are compared.

Details

When some profiles (combinations of test results) are never verified, the data say nothing about how many diseased subjects they contain (Gustafson, 2015), and the sensitivities and specificities depend on it. If neither test declares a never-verified profile positive, however, the unknown diseased subjects are missed by both tests: they lower the two sensitivities by the same factor, and the ratio of the sensitivities does not change. The same holds for the false positive rates. These ratios therefore tell how the tests compare, for example that one detects 15% more diseased subjects than the other, without any assumption on the never-verified profiles; the posterior probability that a ratio is greater than 1 tells which test is more sensitive, or less specific. Tests or rules that declare a never-verified profile positive are left out.

The ratios depend on the odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile, which the data cannot estimate: they are computed for one fixed value, odds_ratio (by default 1, verification that does not depend on the disease).

Why the ratios are estimated by the data. Let \(\omega_t\) be the frequency of profile \(t\), \(\psi_t\) the proportion of diseased in it, known from the data for the profiles with verified subjects, and \(\pi\) the prevalence, which depends on the unknown \(\psi_t\) of the never-verified profiles. For a rule \(R\) that declares no never-verified profile positive, $$A_R = \sum_{t: r_R(t) = 1} \omega_t \psi_t, \qquad B_R = \sum_{t: r_R(t) = 1} \omega_t (1 - \psi_t)$$ are known, and \(Se_R = A_R / \pi\), \(1 - Sp_R = B_R / (1 - \pi)\). For two such rules the unknown prevalence cancels out in the ratios $$rTPR = \frac{Se_R}{Se_{R'}} = \frac{A_R}{A_{R'}}, \qquad rFPR = \frac{1 - Sp_R}{1 - Sp_{R'}} = \frac{B_R}{B_{R'}},$$ which are therefore estimated from the data alone (Alonzo, 2005; Pepe and Alonzo, 2001; Schatzkin et al., 1987). \(rTPR > 1\) means that \(R\) is more sensitive than \(R'\), \(rFPR > 1\) that it is less specific, whatever the proportion of diseased in the never-verified profiles.

The accuracy is defined for a rule \(R\), which declares a subject positive or negative from the response profile \(t\), the vector of the results of the tests: \(r_R(t) = 1\) if the profile is declared positive, 0 otherwise. A single test is the rule "this test is positive". The quantities depend on the prevalence \(\pi = P(D = 1)\) and on the distribution of the profiles in the diseased, \(\theta_{1,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 1)\), and in the healthy, \(\theta_{0,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 0)\):

  • sensitivity (Se): $$Se_R = P(R \textrm{ positive} \mid D = 1) = \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{1,t},$$ the proportion of diseased subjects that the rule declares positive. It is also called the true positive rate (TPR);

  • specificity (Sp): $$Sp_R = P(R \textrm{ negative} \mid D = 0) = 1 - \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{0,t},$$ the proportion of healthy subjects that the rule declares negative; \(1 - Sp_R\) is the false positive rate (FPR);

  • positive predictive value (PPV): $$PPV_R = P(D = 1 \mid R \textrm{ positive}) = \frac{\pi\, Se_R}{\pi\, Se_R + (1 - \pi)(1 - Sp_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared positive is diseased;

  • negative predictive value (NPV): $$NPV_R = P(D = 0 \mid R \textrm{ negative}) = \frac{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R}{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R + \pi\, (1 - Se_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared negative is healthy.

Sensitivity and specificity describe the rule and do not depend on the prevalence; the predictive values describe what a result means for a subject, and change with the prevalence of the population. For combined rules, such as any_positive(), the accuracy depends on the joint distribution of the tests, not only on their individual sensitivities and specificities (Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997; Vacek, 1985).

Each quantity is computed from every posterior draw of \(\pi\), \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\). The results report its posterior mean and median and an equal-tailed credible interval with probability level.

References

Alonzo, T. A. (2005). Verification bias-corrected estimators of the relative true and false positive rates of two binary screening tests. Statistics in Medicine, 24(3), 403–417. doi:10.1002/sim.1959

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Pepe, M. S. and Alonzo, T. A. (2001). Comparing disease screening tests when true disease status is ascertained only for screen positives. Biostatistics, 2(3), 249–260. doi:10.1093/biostatistics/2.3.249

Schatzkin, A., Connor, R. J., Taylor, P. R. and Bunnag, B. (1987). Comparing new and old screening tests when a reference procedure cannot be performed on all screenees. American Journal of Epidemiology, 125(4), 672–678. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a114580

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

See also

accuracy_bounds(), compare_tests()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_study(n = 2000, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0, 0.9, 0.9, 1))
d <- baysesp_data(d, tests = c("A", "B"), verified = "verified", disease = "disease")
fit <- baysesp(d, saturated(unverified_prevalence_prior = elicit_beta(0.03, 0.06)),
               seed = 1)
accuracy_ratios(fit, rules = list("A", "B", any_positive()))
#>                     quantity      mean    median     lower     upper
#> 1            TPR[A] / TPR[B] 1.1257133 1.1244594 1.0542048 1.2023885
#> 2            FPR[A] / FPR[B] 3.0049022 2.9699549 2.3516809 3.8055525
#> 3 TPR[A] / TPR[any positive] 0.9038729 0.9045453 0.8711354 0.9325346
#> 4 FPR[A] / FPR[any positive] 0.7841286 0.7845892 0.7366917 0.8283043
#> 5 TPR[B] / TPR[any positive] 0.8035287 0.8044312 0.7618647 0.8420550
#> 6 FPR[B] / FPR[any positive] 0.2640154 0.2639032 0.2171594 0.3151010
#>   probability
#> 1      0.9995
#> 2      1.0000
#> 3      0.0000
#> 4      0.0000
#> 5      0.0000
#> 6      0.0000
# }
